1: Practical three and four. Know your data: a student's guide to spotting data types and structure in your own dataset. Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio levels; discrete and continuous values; structured and semi structured data; text; and time series.
2: What we will cover: five simple questions that reveal how any column in your dataset behaves. One, nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio: the four levels of measurement for any variable. Two, discrete versus continuous: counting numbers versus measuring numbers. Three, structured versus semi structured: how neatly your data fits into rows and columns. Four, text data basics: working with free form sentences and words. And five, time series behaviour: spotting trend and seasonality over time.
3: Levels of measurement. Ask: are the values labels or numbers, and can you rank them or measure real distance? Nominal: categories with no natural order, like gender, blood type, city or product category. Ordinal: categories that can be ranked, but the gaps are not equal, like satisfaction as low, medium or high, education level, or a star rating. Interval: numbers with equal spacing but no true zero, like temperature in Celsius, I Q score or the calendar year. Ratio: numbers with equal spacing and a true zero that means none, like height, weight, age, income or the number of items sold.
4: A quick test to find the level in your column. Look at the column's values. If they are words or categories, ask: can the categories be ranked in order? If there is no order, it is nominal. If there is an order, it is ordinal. If they are numbers, ask: does zero mean none at all, a true zero? If there is no true zero, it is interval. If there is a true zero, it is ratio. A tip: a true zero means zero truly means nothing exists. Zero income means no income. But zero degrees Celsius does not mean no temperature, so temperature is interval, not ratio.
5: Discrete versus continuous. Both are numeric. The test is whether you can count the values or must measure them. Discrete values are countable, whole numbers, and you could list every possible value: zero, one, two, three. Examples: the number of children in a family, the number of orders placed, the number of clicks on a page, the count of defective items. Continuous values are measurable and can take any number in a range, including decimals. Examples: height of one seventy two point four centimetres, temperature of thirty six point six degrees, time taken of two point three five seconds, weight of fifty eight point two kilograms. The test: can you count it as one, two, three, with nothing in between? Or could the value fall anywhere between two numbers?
6: Structured versus semi structured data. Look at how the file itself is laid out, not just the values inside it. Structured data has fixed rows and columns, every record has the same fields, ready for a spreadsheet or S Q L table. For example, a table with I D, name and score. Examples: an Excel sheet, a C S V file, a S Q L database table. Semi structured data has tags, keys or labels for organisation, but no fixed table shape, and fields can differ between records. In the J S O N example, one record has a name, an age and a list of tags. Examples: J S O N, X M L, log files, and emails with headers.
7: Text data: the basics. Free form text columns need to be broken down before you can analyse them. One, raw text: a full sentence, comment or paragraph exactly as written, like a product review or survey response. Two, tokens: text broken into individual words or symbols so a computer can count and compare them. Three, structure levels: text is organised in layers, from character to word to sentence to paragraph to document. Four, free text versus categorical: open ended answers, like what did you like, differ from fixed label text columns, like yes or no, or city. A worked example: the sentence I loved this product, with an exclamation mark, becomes the tokens I, loved, this, product, and the exclamation mark.
8: Time series behaviour: trend and seasonality. If your data has a date or time column, check whether values move over time in these two ways. Trend is the overall direction the values move over the long run, upward, downward or flat, ignoring short term wiggles. Seasonality is a pattern that repeats at fixed intervals, for example every twelve months, every week, every day, caused by seasons, holidays or habits. The chart shows monthly sales over two years. To check, plot the values against their date or time. A rising or falling line is a trend. Regular repeating bumps are seasonality.
9: Cheat sheet: questions to ask your dataset. Are the values words or numbers? That tells you categorical versus numeric. Can the categories be ranked? Nominal versus ordinal. Does zero mean none at all? Interval versus ratio. Can you count every possible value? Discrete versus continuous. Is it in neat rows and columns, or tags and keys? Structured versus semi structured. Is the column open ended sentences? Then it is text data. Is there a repeating date or time column? Then it is a time series, with trend and seasonality to check.
